speakerposition: topic
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, March 22, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Winters-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act to provide that the Minister of Finance may pay a higher contribution for a portion of the highway in a province not exceeding ten per centum thereof; to *extend contributions to costs incurred up to December 31, 1960 and to terminate all contributions on May 31, 1961; and to provide further that the aggregate of all expenditures under the act may be increased to a maximum of two hundred .and fifty million dollars.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is one of those matters which is resumed after considerable delay, occasioned mainly by the Easter recess. The last time we discussed it was on March 22. I said a few words prior to the adjournment on that day in which I had just got to the point where I was seeking to demonstrate that the proposal now before the house is neither adequate to ensure the completion of the trans-Canada highway by the date mentioned in the resolution, namely, December 31, 1960, nor is it fair as between provinces which are participating members under the trans-Canada highway agreement. This resolution, if it carries, and the bill which will be based on it, would confine the increased federal contribution to 90 per cent of the now uncompleted portion of the highway, not exceeding 10 per cent of the total mileage in any one province. That will have the effect-and I refer particularly to British Columbia and Ontario, the two provinces with the highest per-mile construction costs -that they will not receive a federal contribution which goes anything like far enough to take account of their actual per-mile construction costs.
It also has this further effect. It will penalize a province which has pressed on with the construction of the highway under the existing agreement because in the proposed legislation there is no feature which takes account of completed mileage. In the introductory remarks of the parliamentary assistant to the minister it was made clear that this resolution and the legislation to be based on it have reference only to the uncompleted portion of the highway, with the result that for those portions of the highway already completed through the mountainous area and through the rock and lake area of Ontario, or any of the other difficult portions of the highway which have already been constructed, the provinces are to get no additional reimbursement. If the province has been vigorous in its construction program in the past, as I say, it is now penalized to the extent that it gets only up to 10 per cent of the cost of the remaining mileage at the increased rate whereas a province which may have lagged behind in its construction program in the past and therefore has a bigger mileage uncompleted, can get up to 10 per cent of the total portion at the increased rate of 90 per cent contribution by the dominion government. That is something which seems to be a discrimination against those provinces which have pursued a vigorous construction program.
Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, the proposal seems to me to leave out of account altogether

the obligation on the dominion government- and I use the term "obligation" deliberately- to ensure that there will be at least one trans-Canada highway completed with the least possible delay. I think it is an obligation of the national government to ensure that there shall be a national highway from coast to coast in Canada, it is perfectly true that the objective involves-and rightly so-the co-operation of the provinces because road building and jurisdiction over roads when built are provincial responsibilities. But I think it is the responsibility of this government to ensure that the road is completed and that it is possible for the provinces to complete the road.
I know for a fact what the situation is with respect to my own province. This matter is not dependent upon what particular government may be in office in a province. I am sure that other members know with respect to their provinces-and it is the situation with respect to mine-that their provinces now are extended nearly to the limit with respect to their commitments on road construction. They have extremely heavy obligations. In British Columbia we have many developmental roads which need to be constructed and many secondary roads which need to be brought up to an adequate standard. The provinces cannot disregard their obligations in this field in order to go ahead and devote all their energies within their road building commitments to the completion of the trans-Canada highway simply because the dominion government says, "We want you to do this and we will pay a portion of the cost but only after December 31, 1960".
The provinces have too many other pressing commitments with respect to road building to allow them to be prejudiced because they can only get a dominion contribution under this program within a limited period. They find themselves in the position where they are only going to get a very limited dominion contribution in any event, that is up to 90 per cent of 10 per cent of the presently uncompleted road, but nothing over 50 per cent for the remainder. I believe that to expect the provinces faced with very heavy per mile construction costs on the portion of the road which exceeds 10 per cent of the total mileage in the province to drop everything else and devote the necessary effort to that uncompleted portion within this period will not make it possible for the road to be completed within the time contemplated. I feel, therefore, that this government should take a new look at the problem in conjunction with the provinces to work out some scheme which would be
Trans-Canada Highway Act more within the resources of the provinces to complete within the time contemplated.
We are left, sir, with this inescapable fact. We are now virtually at the end of the first seven year period of the agreement and we have not got anything like a completed first class trans-Canada highway. The dominion government went a certain distance towards accepting this responsibility in the first agreement, but it did not accept its full responsibility. How can it be denied that there is a responsibility today to see that steps are taken to complete a trans-Canada highway in this year 1956 when you contrast our position with the position in the United States where, with greater wealth and a greater population, they have had a national highway system for many years? In view of the comments that have been made on the present proposal by provincial highways ministers, in view of the facts we ourselves know about the difficulties in connection with the construction of these roads and their tremendous costs, I believe not only that this proposal is inadequate with respect to the one road but that we are stopping short of assuming the full responsibility which the central government should assume with respect to a highway system generally.
Where so much depends on the development programs which are followed, so much depends on the opening up of new territory and so much of the cost of that development in providing the physical plan and equipment -roads are certainly part of the physical plan and equipment necessary for development-rests with the provinces while the nation as a whole receives in large measure the general benefit from such a development program, and the federal treasury benefits to the greatest extent as a result of the increased revenues which accrue from these developments, it seems to me antiquated thinking to say that the dominion government is only partially responsible and only for one road. I am convinced, without going into the details, that the time has long gone by when this whole question of a national highway system, to which the dominion government will make a contribution on an agreed basis with the provinces, should be faced and solved if a fair apportionment as between the dominion and the provinces of the cost of development is to be adequately made.
So I suggest to the minister in all earnestness that he take a further look at the problem. I believe that this resolution falls short of meeting the requirements of the situation, both with respect to the one road and because I believe it is unsound thinking to concentrate all our attention on the problem of a single trans-Canada road and that it

Trans-Canada Highway Act is time we were thinking and planning in terms of a national highway system.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
We in this group are pleased that the government has seen fit to extend provisions for the building of the trans-Canada highway. Certainly a great deal has already been accomplished in the time that has been spent in the building of that highway. I think the action taken by parliament and by the provinces will provide a genuine service to the people of this country.
Although a good deal has been accomplished much remains to be done. As was pointed out by the Department of Public Works in a statement made on January 5, of the 4,580 miles already in existence, apart from the road going through the province of Quebec, only. 1,315 miles have been paved to date. In other words 30 per cent has been paved to trans-Canada standards and 1,727 miles remain to be graded and surfaced. In other words, 37 per cent of the mileage has still to be paved. So while we have made considerable progress we still have a long way to go.
Hon. members sometimes wonder whether provincial governments, composed of parties different from the party which composes the federal government in power, will in fact co-operate with the federal government on the various projects. I think the co-operation of all provincial governments that have taken part in this program, regardless of their particular party affiliation, indicates that the provinces generally are anxious to proceed with this project and to follow it through to completion.
Because I come from Saskatchewan I am naturally particularly pleased with what I consider to be the excellent showing made by that province on its portion of the trans-Canada highway. As I read the statement released by the Department of Public Works, Saskatchewan has now paved more miles of the trans-Canada highway within its borders than has any other province. I realize that that is not a completely fair comparison because certain other provinces do not have the same mileage and certain other provinces have a more difficult and expensive construction program through terrain that is not nearly as accessible as the terrain in Saskatchewan. Considering Saskatchewan's relatively meagre resources I think the province is to be commended on taking what amounts to a lead in proceeding with this very important project.
The hon. member for Kamloops made one statement which I do not think is correct and which I hope is not correct. He suggested that the provinces which have proceeded with the building of this highway are


now going to be penalized by the terms of this resolution. I hope the hon. member is wrong in saying that, because I fully agree that any province which has co-operated and has built a large portion of its road mileage should in no way be penalized as a result of having co-operated with the federal government. On the face of it, such a penalty would not be fair. If such a penalty were levied by the provisions of this new act, I would be fearful that future co-operation with any of the provinces in federal undertakings would be jeopardized. I merely express the hope that when the legislation is drafted and presented to this house no province will be penalized in any way because it has proceeded with its portion of the highway in good faith and in full co-operation with the federal government. I observe that the parliamentary assistant is nodding his head in the affirmative so I take it that whatever the precise provisions of the new bill are there will be no penalty to any province which has acted in good faith.
I think a project like the trans-Canada highway and the further development of our roads is not something that can be considered as a net expense or a loss to the country; rather I consider such an expenditure by the people of Canada in an adequate highway program an investment that will pay dividends in the future, an investment that will in fact be self-liquidating. I believe it will benefit the people of this nation through greater productivity that will more than offset the actual cost of such a program.
We know that the roads in all provinces of Canada are inadequate and leave much to be desired. If we had an adequate highway system in this modern age of automobile transportation huge sums of money would be saved, I am sure, through a saving in gasoline consumption, a saving in repairs to automobiles and trucks and a saving in labour because transportation would be speeded up.
I believe that the use of new roads to develop mining areas would increase the wealth of this nation and would add to our general prosperity and economic well being. I think the federal government should consider spending relatively large sums of money to promote the building of highways that will open up new mining areas in the great northern part of this country. I think that such development roads would increase the wealth production of our nation to a degree that would offset many-fold the cost of such roads.
I am not well acquainted with all the development roads that might be undertaken, but having some knowledge of the

province of Saskatchewan I would suggest that probably three development roads should be built in that province. I suggest an extension of the highway north through Lac la Ronge to Uranium city; an extension of highway No. 4 north of North Battleford also to Uranium city, both highways opening up relatively large and important new mining areas. I would also suggest a development road from Nipawin to Flin Flon to open up a further area. These are the types of roads which if proceeded with would not be a net expense but would be a self-liquidating investment in the future.
Our country depends for a substantial part of its prosperity on the tourist industry. In 1954 our tourist industry earned more than $300 million. I do not think any hon. member would deny that if we had a better highway system in Canada we could increase our tourist industry by a substantial amount. In view of all these considerations I suggest that the government should take a new look at the highway program and should be prepared to invest federal money in the building of an adequate road system in Canada, not as something that would be a net expenditure or a net loss but as something that would be an extremely important investment in the future of this nation. .
One only needs to point out that at the present time it is estimated that there are four million automobiles in Canada. As far as the number of automobiles is concerned, it is theoretically possible to transport all Canadians in automobiles at one given time. The excellent brief presented to the Minister of Trade and Commerce by the Canadian automobile association pointed out just how important the automobile industry is to our nation. It stated that one person out of every seven owes his employment to the automobile industry. With an industry of such proportions I thing it is well that the government should take active steps to encourage its development. Of course the first essential would be to encourage the development of an adequate highway program.
Somebody may say, "Let us leave it to the provinces, let us leave it to the municipalities". But as a nation we have been leaving it to the municipalities and to the provinces in this field as we have in so many other fields, with I suggest inadequate results. I submit that the provinces and municipalities are already bearing their full share of the burden of building highways. I have in my hand statistics showing the estimated amount of money to be spent on roads in Canada this year. It is estimated that provincial and municipal governments combined will spend
Trans-Canada Highway Act $535 million, while the federal government's total road budget in all its departments will be only $27 million.
When one realizes that the federal government gets the lion's share of taxation revenue he will understand that the provinces have undertaken a most burdensome part of the cost of building roads in this country. The federal budget for this year is estimated at $4,650 million; the provincial budgets for 1955 totalled $1,360 million and the municipal budgets for the last year for which I was able to obtain statistics, 1952, totalled $950 million. It will be seen from those figures that out of each dollar of tax revenue the federal government gets 67 cents, the ten provincial governments combined get 19 cents, while all municipal governments, rural, village, town and city, get only 14 cents of the taxation dollar. I suggest that in all fairness the federal government should consider bearing a larger proportion of the cost of road construction in this country. The provinces are already doing a good deal while the federal government is doing relatively little.
One of the reasons why the provinces are unable to build roads to adequate standards and to have an adequate road mileage is the fact that the number of miles of road related to each provincial budget is not the same as the number of miles of road related to the budgets of other provinces. In other words, some of the poorer provinces in Canada have the largest road mileage to service. Saskatchewan has more miles of improved roads than any other province in Canada. The 1952 highway statistics published by the dominion bureau of statistics give the improved road mileages as follows:
Miles
Saskatchewan	 100,000
Ontario	   74,000
Alberta	 52,800
Manitoba	 17,500
In other words, Saskatchewan has as many miles of improved roads as Alberta and Manitoba combined. Saskatchewan is relatively one of the poorer provinces of this country and certainly when we consider its road obligations it is unable to adequately service 100,000 miles of improved roads. In other words, if Canadians living in all the provinces are to have adequate roads it is essential that the federal government put some real money into a national road building program.
We can take a lead in this connection from the United States. The United States began its federal road program as long ago as 1912. In 1912 the United States government appropriated a certain sum of money to pay one-third of the cost of constructing roads over which the mail was carried. The mail routes
2946	HOUSE OF
Trans-Canada Highway Act in the United States composed most of the important roads in that country. In 1916, four years later, there was a large appropriation of $75 million to be spent over a period of four years on road development.
The United States has gone on year after year to increase the amount of federal money spent on roads. The amount of money spent by the United States government on roads is not confined to one trans-American highway, one road across the country; it is not confined to main highways. The road program in the United States provides money for main interstate highways, for improved highways within states, for farm to market roads, roads over which school buses travel and roads over which mail is carried. The result is that every single mile of road in the United States of any importance has in its construction a certain amount of federal money.
Any of us who have travelled in the United States, and I am sure we all have at one time or another, cannot help but be impressed with the tremendous highway system they have in that country. No one would suggest that Canada could afford to match the United States program dollar for dollar, but I submit that Canada should be able to match the United States program at least in proportion to our population and that we in Canada should provide federal expenditures on roads not less in proportion to our population than is now being spent in the United States on that basis.

speechtext:
No, I am not suggesting that, but I do suggest that the Canadian government should be doing much more that it is now doing by way of providing money for roads. I do not think it is necessary at all


for the federal government to encroach on the field of gasoline taxation in order to provide money for roads. I have already quoted statistics which I think show that the federal government now takes 67 cents out of every tax dollar. In my opinion the federal government has never been short of fields of taxation and there is no need for it to extend its fields of taxation in order to provide money for such a project.
The hon. member wants me to tell him where I think we can get some money. I believe it is indicated that the Minister of Finance will have almost $300 million extra this year in the form of taxes owed by corporations last year, which money will go into current revenue. I am suggesting that the federal government could match on a population basis the money paid for roads by the government of the United States without increasing taxation in this country in any way, shape or form.
I should like to go on to point out some more details of the United States program. The United States government spends money for a system of primary roads. They have 216,000 miles of rural highways and 18,800 miles of urban highways. The appropriation for the year ending June 30, 1956, for this primary system will be $315 million. If Canada would spend the same amount on a population basis we would be spending something over $28 million, assuming our population to be approximately 9 per cent of that of the United States. If we spent it on the same proportionate mileage, we would be spending such a sum on 19,500 miles of primary roads in this country.
The United States for the same year spent money on 483,000 miles of the secondary highway system. The secondary highway system includes farm to market roads, rural mail routes and school bus routes, and on that secondary system the United States has appropriated $210 million. If Canada spent the same proportionate amount, we would spend $18,900,000 on such a secondary system, or on 43,500 miles in our country.
The urban system, which is also included in the primary system to which I have referred, constitutes 18,812 miles. This year the United States will spend on its urban system $175 million. This is money spent by the federal government of the United States to help take the highways through their large urban centres. Taking highways through heavily populated cities, of course, is very expensive. To enable the cities and the states bear the cost, $175 million is appropriated for this purpose. If we did the same in Canada, we would appropriate for that purpose $15,750,000 on a comparable mileage of 1,700 miles.

The interstate highway system, including the large expressways and the trunk highways in the United States, are limited to 40,000 miles. For this year the federal government will spend $175 million. If Canada did the same, we would appropriate $15,750,000 for this purpose, or for a mileage of 3,600.

speechtext: They do it by taxation.

The United States government is spending on all its road systems, for the year ending June 30, 1956, $875 million. On a proportionate population basis, Canada, to equal the expenditures of the United States, should be appropriating $78,750,000 for this purpose. Even if we appropriated this larger sum of money, it would in no way mean a comparable improvement in our highways, because we have so many more miles of roads for our population than has the United States. If we did it on the same proportionate mileage we would be spending money to assist a system of 68,300 miles of roads this year, rather than something under 5,000 miles, expenditures for which are being provided by the resolution that is now under discussion.
I am suggesting that our federal government could do much more in the way of providing moneys in the building of an adequate road system in our country. The government of the United States not only provides substantial sums of money for its tremendous road system in that country but does it on a formula that, I suggest, is very fair. It provides grants to the states based on the area of each state, based on the population of each state and based on the road mileage within each state. Because the federal government has provided money on that basis, the relatively poor states, the states with sparse populations, obtain a larger proportion of the money they spend on roads from the federal treasury.
I have here the estimates of the amounts of money spent during the past year on roads in three of the states. The total expenditure in North Dakota was just over $13 million, and of this $13 million 50 per cent, or $6,500,000, was provided by the federal treasury. In the state of Montana, a state with a small population, out of a total expenditure of $22 million, $13,500,000 was provided by the federal treasury, or 61 per cent. In the state of Wyoming, with a population even less than that of Montana, for a total expenditure of $9,300,000, $6 million, or 65 per cent, was provided from payments by the federal treasury.
I wish to point out that the federal government in the United States does not control 67509-187
Trans-Canada Highway Act the letting of contracts in the construction of the roads in any way. The building of roads and the supervising of maintenance of roads are responsibilities under the full control and authority of each state. If such a program were offered to the provinces of Canada, there would be no need to interfere in any way with provincial jurisdiction. As a matter of fact, every precaution should be taken not to interfere with provincial jurisdiction. But I am suggesting that in the interests of the development of our country, in the interests of making our country more prosperous, we should be providing larger sums from the federal treasury to provincial governments.
I do not think the minister or his parliamentary assistant could estimate the amount of money that will be necessary for road construction in Canada within the next 20 years, or within the next ten years, or within any future period. I do not think any survey has ever been made of the road needs and the requirements of this nation. I suggest that the first thing the government should do in preparing to undertake a comprehensive road program is to make a survey of our road needs for a substantial period into the future, perhaps a survey of the prospective road needs for the next 20 years, and of what our nation needs in the way of road development in order that it can have its maximum economic development within the next 20 years.
Such a survey should, I suggest, be made after we have determined our likely road needs for a substantial period in the future. Then I suggest the federal government should decide what our road program should be and what our target should be for a shorter period, shall we say, for a four-year period, for a term of office-the usual term of office for any federal parliament-to set forth the road program and certain objectives for the completion of such a program, and then be prepared to advance money to the provinces to ensure that such a program is fulfilled.
I believe we are falling behind in productive development in many ways. If we are going to keep advancing in the future, as far as wealth production is concerned, if we are to advance in the future at a rate that will allow this nation to keep up with and to keep ahead of the rate of advance in the U.S.S.R., then I suggest that one of the essential things for the future peacetime development of Canada is an adequate road program. The federal government is doing very little in the way of providing funds for a road program for Canada.
I would suggest that such a road program should have four essential features. We should
2948	HOUSE OF
Trans-Canada Highway Act provide federal moneys, not just for one trans-Canada highway, but for trans-Canada highways. At this time there certainly should be provision for the construction of at least a second trans-Canada highway following a northern route, in western Canada from Winnipeg to Saskatoon to Edmonton and I believe it is through the Yellowhead pass-the northern route-down to Vancouver in British Columbia. We should have more than one trans-Canada highway. The federal government should be providing money for roads going north and south. We might call them, if you like, international roads-Canadian roads going north and south meeting roads in the United States coming up to the Canadian boundary. From a provincial standpoint, those roads have as much importance to the economy of each province as does a road going east and west. That is the second thing the government should do, provide money for a north-south road program.
The third thing I should like to see is the provision of federal government money to assist the provinces to assist in turn the municipalities in the development of interurban roads, roads between cities within a province that have little to do with connecting roads either trans-Canada or north and south. Under this general heading I would suggest the use of federal money to provide adequate farm to market roads. Because a Canadian happens to be a farmer and happens to live a long distance from the trans-Canada highway or a long distance from a provincial highway is no reason why the federal government should not be looking towards his well being in the future as far as servicing him with an adequate road is concerned. I do not think the rural residents of any province in Canada that you wish to mention will have access to modern roads and highways until the federal government provides some money for the building of farm to market roads through grants to the provinces.

bill and I am not in a position to say whether or not that statement is correct. The resolution indicates a revision of the terms of the present agreement. Let me put it on the record. It is as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act to provide that the Minister of Finance may pay a higher contribution for a portion of the highway in a province not exceeding ten per centum thereof: to extend contributions to costs incurred up to December 31, 1960 and to terminate all contributions on May 31, 1961; and to provide further that the aggregate of all expenditures under the act may be increased to a maximum of $250 million.
We are all very pleased, Mr. Chairman, that the minister is reconsidering the whole matter of highway construction. I hardly think there has been a year when this problem has been under discussion in the house that I have not indicated my anxiety to the minister as to when the road would be completed. We in western Canada particularly are very concerned as to the time when the highway is going to be completed because it enters materially into our economic existence. I remember making a wager when the legislation was first introduced, to the extent of $10, I believe, that the road would not be completed in the time specified in the agreement. Now what do we find? We find that the road is not 50 per cent completed. I am going to suggest now, Mr. Chairman, that the road will not be completed by the end of the new term, December 31, 1960.

I would agree with the hon. member, and believe me, this is no gamble. You only gamble when there is a chance that you will lose, but in this case that is not so. I think the construction of the trans-Canada highway is probably one of the most important projects under way in this country. In fact, I think it is even much more important than the St. Lawrence seaway because it will have a greater effect on the total economy of our country.
I have here a clipping from the Western Producer of May 4, 1950. I recall that I put the article on Hansard at that time and I want to repeat some portions of it now to

show what was the common opinion about the importance of this highway at that date. The article reads in part:
Course of the highway across the west was never a very important issue, really. The big question was not where, but when the road would be built. Whether it traversed the flat, often treeless and to some travellers monotonous south country or along the more scenic northern path, the trans-Canada road was, and is, of vital importance to western Canada. It will be a strong link between the industrial east and the agricultural west and constitute a sound beachhead on the trade and geographic barrier separating the two. From the standpoint of national defence, the highway is imperative now that Canada is at the crossroads of world history.
There are one or two things mentioned there to which I should like to make reference. I should like to deal first with the beachhead on the trade and geographic barriers separating the east and west. I have often thought, and have so expressed my opinion in the house, that one of the things that has caused a lagging in the construction of the highway is that it has been in the interests of the railways-certainly it has proved to be in their interests-to see that the highway was not completed. In my judgment that has been one of the major factors in holding back the completion of the highway not only during the first term of the agreement but for many years prior thereto. If for no other reason the highway should be completed as quickly as possible in order to develop the economic position of our country and certainly in order to take care of national needs in time of emergency.
We have an emergency coming now in the form of a possible railway strike. Of course everybody is saying that we should not have a strike because it would paralyse transportation in all of Canada. Of course it would, but who is to blame for that situation? Certainly it is not the worker. The ones who are to blame for such a situation are the federal government who have failed in seeing that another means of transcontinental transportation has not been completed which could be of service not only in times such as these but in times of national emergency arising from a war or other like causes.

Let me say something about the construction of this highway, Mr. Chairman. You will recall that when we first discussed the standards of this highway I made objection at that time. I pointed out that a two-lane highway across this country was not good enough and that the standards with which the roads were being built would in all probability not be sufficient to carry the loads that would be carried on that road. When these specifications were first implemented I think probably they were better specifications than those for any other roads that were being built in Canada at that time. But this was a tremendous project. This was a project which was going to cost millions of dollars. It was one which, in my judgment at least, was to provide an alternative mode of transportation to that provided by the railways. It was to provide transportation by trucks which would carry at least a portion of our freight and other things of that nature

across the country. It was going to be subjected to very strenuous use and it was a road that would have to be built to withstand it. It was my judgment then, as it is now, that this road should be a four-lane highway or at least that provision should have been made for a possible four-lane highway. When they were buying the right of way I believe they should have bought sufficient land in order to be able to extend that road to a four-lane highway when the necessity arose. But that was never done. I also think that the gravel base is not sufficiently deep and that it is not sufficiently compact to carry the loads that it will be required to carry. I think the hard surface on the road is not sufficiently thick to carry the weight that will be put upon it. The provinces now-and particularly the province of Alberta-are using much better standards in building their main roads than that which was used in connection with the trans-Canada highway.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak very briefly on this matter because I think it is one of the most important issues which will come before parliament this session. The purpose of the resolution is simply to provide federal assistance to the the provinces in a financial way, to help them finish the trans-Canada highway at the earliest possible date. I am quite sure that hon. members of all parties will support the principle of the proposal.
I think anyone who travels across this great country of ours today must be shocked
16. 1956
Trans-Canada Highway Act at the appalling condition of some of our main highways. I think anyone who travels across Canada, must also be shocked when he realizes that 89 years after confederation, he still cannot travel from eastern Canada to western Canada or vice versa on a Canadian highway. These conditions prevail despite the fact that since 1945 we have had booming economic conditions, and despite the fact that we have had the greatest period of economic development in our history.
I think it was in 1949 that parliament brought in legislation under which the federal government would pay up to 50 per cent of the cost of a trans-Canada highway, and all of us welcomed it as progressive legislation. Seven years have elapsed since that time and the progress which we have made has been disappointingly slow; indeed it has been frustrating in the extreme.
As was pointed out by the parliamentary assistant in his speech before Easter, the trans-Canada highway is 4,580 miles in length and yet at this moment only 1,600 miles, or approximately 35 per cent, have been completed despite the fact that the whole project was supposed to have been finished in this present year. I suggest that the project to date is a colossal failure, in view of the fact that only 35 per cent of the original target has been reached. Surely this construction record should emphasize to parliament and to the country the glaring weaknesses of our Canadian highway system.
The legislation which is before us today is going to be useful, but certainly in no way is it going to get at the crux of our highway difficulties. I think, Mr. Chairman, most hon. members would agree that our difficulties go back to 1867. The British North America Act left highway construction up to the provinces and that fact has resulted in a serious financial tangle. While the provinces have jurisdiction over roads, only the federal government has the financial resources necessary to build the kind of roads that Canadians want. I say also that our constitution has meant that instead of having one over-all, comprehensive highway program, we have ten different programs in Canada today. They are seldom integrated and often conflicting; at times they are subject to local and provincial political thinking. I think it is quite obvious that the fathers of confederation envisaged no highway problem such as we have today in 1956. Because of our vast distances and our sparse populations, the municipal and provincial governments simply cannot build the kind of highways that we need. I think that sooner or later parliament is going to have to face up squarely to that fact.
Our Canadian highway situation is completely unique. To the best of my knowledge

Trans-Canada Highway Act every other country in the western world builds its highways on a national basis. I think this is true in Europe, South America, North America and even in Mexico, which we sometimes look upon as a slightly backward country.
It was pointed out earlier in this debate that the United States has a system for building highways which is far superior to our own. In the United States aid is usually given up to 50 per cent, not only on state but also on municipal highways. Sometimes that aid is as much as 80 per cent. As a result of this policy, the United States has a superb national system of highways.
I do not think I am biased in saying that the federal government has displayed far too little interest in this national and crucial problem. I say that it has avoided its responsibility by leaning on the technical excuse of constitutional responsibility. I do not think that Canadian highway development can any longer be held up for that reason. We have excellent precedents in matters affecting our national welfare where the federal government has acted, despite the fact that primary responsibility rested with the provinces. I remind the house of old age pensions, family allowances, grants to universities and the like. Surely the day has finally come when this parliament should consider taking the same kind of action where highways are concerned.
Some may ask, "How would you pay for it?" I believe the hon. member for Hamilton South asked that question this afternoon. A highway program would have to be paid for, of course. If it had to be paid for by a federal gasoline tax, I do not think too many Canadians would object, if as a result they had decent roads to travel over. I would remind this house that in the last four years the federal government has taken $700 million from the motorists of Canada in excise taxes, sales taxes on automobiles and tires, customs tariffs on imported cars, etc. I would also remind the house- that last year the federal government spent only the sum of $27 million on highways; therefore I say that the income and the outgoing expenditures are not in line. I think we Canadians have shown a disconcerting lack of vision and imagination in building highways.
I say again that the resolution before us is welcome, but surely we should go a good deal further. I call upon this government this afternoon to embark on a bold and aggressive highway program which will actually get construction work under way. Personally I should like to see parliament set up a national highway commission similar

to the one they have in the United States. I believe that the duties of such a highway commission should be fourfold.
First, it should provide federal funds to the provinces on a co-operative basis of not less than 50-50 on all east and west and all north and south roads; that is, on all major roads. In the second place, the commission should provide funds to provincial governments on a co-operative basis for maintenance work. In the third place, the commission should devise a master plan for a national highway system towards which the dominion government and the ten provincial governments could work. Fourth, the commission could standardize construction and engineering specifications.
My own thinking would be similar to the views of other hon. members who have spoken, namely that the actual construction work should be left with the provinces, but grants would definitely remain subject to approval by the commission. I suggest that over a ten-year period the federal government should spend not less than $2,000 million, or approximately $200 million a year. Some hon. members may think that I am not being consistent when I make such a suggestion, but I look upon expenditures for highways, not as dead-weight expenditures but rather as an investment, and a self-liquidating asset. I think the federal government would get its money back in the way of extra returns from tourists and from mineral development.
I submit that a proper highway system is vital to the life of this country. I shall vote for this resolution but I say again that it is certainly not an answer to Canada's highway problems.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like other hon. members who have spoken this afternoon, I have travelled on a number of our highways during the past two years. I was fortunate enough to travel across the country twice, and I have travelled a considerable distance by automobile. Like other hon. members, I was shocked at the condition of a great many of our highways. How we can expect to develop our country, and particularly to attract tourists with the highways we can offer them at present, is to me beyond comprehension.
Today, more than five years after the trans-Canada highway program was started, we find that out of a total of 4,600 miles, which will comprise the highway, as of March 1 only 1,315 miles have been paved and 1,748 miles graded. Each of the provinces participating in the program is lagging behind by about the same proportion.
Why should it be that during five years of unprecedented boom we find that less

than one-third of this highway has been completed? It is simply that the provinces, which have great demands upon them to build roads to serve the people within their own boundaries, do not have funds available to meet their 50 per cent share of the cost. The more they spend upon the trans-Canada highway, the less they have to spend on roads which are their primary concern, and quite naturally they have decided to spend the greater proportion of their highway funds upon roads which are their primary concern.
The present proposal of the government to pay 90 per cent of the cost of not more than 10 per cent of the highway in any province will not get this highway built, for the reason that in each province there is today more than two-thirds of the highway yet to be completed. When this program which the government is proposing is completed, there will still be large gaps which at today's rate of construction will require many years of work before the highway is completed.
I think that we in this parliament, particularly the government, must face up to the hard, cold fact that if this highway is to be built within the foreseeable future, the federal government must assume the financial responsibility for its construction and stop playing around with makeshift methods of trying to get it built.
On grounds of defence alone, the construction of this highway can be justified as a federal responsibility. On the ground of assisting in the development of our natural resources, from which the federal government' is the chief beneficiary, the construction of this highway can be justified as a federal responsibility. On the ground that the present arrangement with the provinces to build the highway has failed dismally, the construction of this highway can be justified as a federal responsibility. In short, if this highway is going to be built in the foreseeable future, the federal government must assume financial responsibility and get' on with the job.
While the proposal which is before us is a move in the right direction, in my estimation it will simply not get the highway built in the next few years. The highway must be built for a number of reasons, and I feel it is up to the federal government to stop fooling around with this important matter. It has done so for five years; it should face the facts and assume its financial responsibility and get on with the job.
In addition to needing badly the trans-Canada highway, this country also needs badly a national highway program by which the federal government would join with the provinces in the building of highways which would
Trans-Canada Highway Act enable us to develop our tourist trade and our natural resources, and also to man properly our defences. Roads into the north, in the western and central part's of Canada and across the maritime provinces, would make available opportunities which would bring new mining fields into production; which would make available new timber resources; which would bring about the construction of pulp and paper mills which could use resources not now available, instead of leaving them to waste; and would permit an expansion in our tourist industry, and to some degree, our fishing and trapping industries as well.
A program for the building of north and south roads not only would bring in many millions of dollars in the form of tourist trade, but there would be extra gasoline, liquor and amusement taxes for the provincial treasuries. Such a program would also provide many millions of dollars in additional corporation and sales taxes for the federal treasury. For that reason I think it is obvious that the building of these roads would be a money-making proposition for the federal government. There would be definite economic advantages which would accrue to the federal government by the building of roads of this kind. If the federal government would join with the provinces to press forward with a program of this kind, there would be possible a development of our tourist industry and of our natural resources as well.
Another thing to be accomplished by the building of these roads would be assistance in the expansion of our manufacturing industries, about which so many speakers have spoken recently in this house. They have pointed out how badly it is needed in this country.
In the past, railway construction and expansion were badly needed to assist in industrial expansion. In exactly the same way today, the building of good highways is needed. Just as we in this country must concentrate on creating an economic atmosphere which will induce new industries to start up and build new factories to process our raw materials, we must build roads by which new industries can receive raw materials and ship finished goods.
As the federal government will be the chief beneficiary from the new taxes that will result from the creation of these new secondary industries, there should be no hesitation on the part of the federal government in contributing-and contributing generously -to the building of these roads, in addition to the trans-Canada highway.
Finally we come to the matter of defence. Because our defences are today stretching

Trans-Canada Highway Act farther and farther north, I think it is obvious that we have to build good north and south highways to provide easy access to our defence installations and to the localities we may very easily have to defend in case of attack. The responsibility in this regard is undoubtedly a federal one. So the federal government, in co-operation with the provinces, must embark on a national highways program to ensure the construction of highways that are needed for the development of our natural resources and our tourist industry, and to make available defence installations in the localities we may have to defend in case of attack. A program of building north and south highways in conjunction with the provinces must be proceeded with immediately.
Such a program, of course, will cost a good deal of money, but I do not believe that such a program should be paid for out of current revenue. It is a program which will enable this country to be developed; it is a program which will benefit future generations; and I believe it is a program which should be financed by bond issues, both federal and provincial. I believe that the people of this country will be willing to finance in such a way a highway program which will make possible the development and the defence of their country.
Recently, the United States announced a $1 billion highway program in which the federal government pays the cost of construction of federal highways and the state governments pay the upkeep. This is the kind of arrangement that has worked very well in practice below the border, and it results in federal highways being built and maintained to the public satisfaction. I believe that such an arrangement for this country would work very well indeed; an arrangement by which the federal government could build the highways and the provincial governments would maintain them, or an arrangement by which the federal and provincial governments could jointly build and maintain these federal highways.
I believe this is a matter which the federal government should look into and study very seriously indeed. It is a matter which can,
I believe, have very beneficial effects for the development of this country. I believe it is essential for the development of our tourist industry, the development of our industrial expansion and the adequate manning of our defences. I urge the federal government to give this matter serious consideration and I feel sure that, having done so, it will come to the conclusion that such a program, in conjunction with the provinces, should be proceeded with in the very near future.

At this time I should like to make a few remarks with reference to this resolution. May I say at the beginning, whilst I recognize that the building of the highways and roads is the responsibility of the provinces, it is my opinion that there should be across this country one federal highway, and the cost of that federal highway should be borne by the federal government.
Dealing directly with the resolution, I may say at the outset that I am going to vote for this resolution, but I am going to do so for one or two reasons. First of all, I welcome the increasing support that the federal government proposes here to give to the provinces, particularly those that have been delayed in trying to carry out their contracts in building this trans-Canada highway.
I do, however, look with some concern on the date for the completion of the highway, May 31. I am not so much concerned about the year 1961 as I am about May 31. I believe that this contract should terminate either at the end of a fiscal period or at the end of a road-building period. For example, as in our case in Newfoundland, it may mean that in some provinces they will be able to continue the building of the trans-Canada highway during the year 1961, but there will be no possibility of ending then, because at that time of the year there is no possibility of conducting any road-building operations.
In Newfoundland, of course, transportation has always been a problem. In the early days, when the major part of the transportation was carried on by ships operating around the coast, it was a necessity to have those ships. Gradually roads were built, and we have reached the point today that our transportation by boat has been tremendously decreased, and therefore we have to rely more on the Canadian National Railways and on our road system. This great increase in the need for transportation has been due, of course, to many things. When I spoke in the house on the speech in reply, I gave to this house some figures showing the increase in traffic in Newfoundland, and that increase has been largely due to a rising standard of living. It has been due to a large increase in productivity and due to a great increase in the amount of trade that Newfoundland does with the mainland. I might say that at the moment Newfoundland is doing $100 million a year more trade with the mainland of Canada than it did with the mainland of Canada prior to 1949.
The provincial government, in trying to provide a highway system for Newfoundland, has made a courageous and very energetic effort. As everybody knows, in an area where

roads have always been inadequate, roadbuilding only generates a further demand for road-building. It is obvious that a great deal of the load has been thrown on to the C.N.R. They too, I agree, have had their problems in trying to cope with this increased traffic, but at the moment they have not been very effective in doing so. In many areas of Newfoundland the requirements that the C.N.R. has been able to provide have not been up to the minimum requirements.
This Trans-Canada Highway Act, which became effective on December 10, 1949, was signed by Newfoundland on June 23, 1950. The length of the proposed route is 610 miles. Over this route, I believe, there is sufficient reason to believe that there is a good argument, from the standpoint of defence, that this road should have been paid for entirely by the federal government. It starts at Port aux Basques, for example, and after 100 miles or so comes into the tremendous United States air force base at Harmon field. It does not go directly there. It by-passes it but a short by-road will take you there. It goes on then to large towns like Stephenville, Corner Brook, Deer Lake, Grand Falls and then on to another major air establishment at Gander. Then it goes on for another couple of hundred miles to two more major air establishments at Argentia and Torbay, and of course thence to the capital of Newfoundland, St. John's.
The road as it was to be built in Newfoundland was to be built in three stages. There was first the rough grading using material along the right of way. Second, there was the strengthening of the sub-grade to withstand axle loads of 18,000 pounds. Third, there was the paving construction. So far we have completed about 200 miles of the first phase. I do not mean to say here that is the only part of the trans-Canada highway over which you can now go. You can go nearly 500 miles but the many miles you can now travel over are due to prior construction.
As to the second phase, we have a great deal of difficulty in getting the right kind of road-building material. It is not very plentiful and it is very expensive. The second phase, strengthening the sub-grade, is a very important part of road building in a country like Newfoundland where over long winter periods you have wide changes in temperature. The result is that if the roadbed is not properly built no paved surface is ever going to last for very long. As to the third phase, paving, we have done no paving on the trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland. Nevertheless, we are anxious to

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the remarks just made by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's indicate very clearly the need for a new approach to a Canadian highway policy. When one considers the unspectacular results of the trans-Canada highway legislation thus far in terms of the needs of this country I think one must feel rather disappointed, to say the least. I believe that as a parliament responsible for the needs and the future of all parts of Canada we have got to look at the problem of highway construction in a more realistic fashion.
I grant you that in 1867, when the fathers of confederation brought forth the legislation which forms the basis of our constitution, a different situation existed altogether. Railways and to a lesser extent canals were the main arteries of communication and transportation in Canada. I think it was the realization on the part of the fathers of this nation, that the railroads would be the links between the various parts of our vast country, that caused them to accept the responsibility for railway construction in Canada. By the same line of reasoning I suggest that today, in view of the fact that highways have become an alternative means of communication and transportation throughout the country, the federal government should be assuming its responsibilities in this regard.
We cannot argue today that roads are strictly a provincial or municipal responsibility. There was a time in our history when 

roads unquestionably were designed primarily to lead to a railroad point, to a port or some point on a canal. Today roads are not only interprovincial but international. Yet the government has failed to take that fact into consideration. Thus we find that the highway policy advocated by the government is shortsighed and fails completely to meet present needs.
I think the Canadian Good Roads Association summed up the situation recently when they pointed out that between the years 1945 and 1953 total motor registrations had increased by 126 per cent, yet during that same time surfaced mileage increased by only 38 per cent. In other words we are not even meeting the present needs of Canada, much less the future needs of Canada. Occasionally we hear political leaders in this country talking about the great future ahead of Canada. I am sure we know that the future belongs to Canada. We know that we are going to have a much greater population in the years that lie ahead. Yet in the highway legislation brought forward by this government there is nothing which would lead anyone to believe that the population of this country was going to increase by one individual in the foreseeable future. If we anticipate a great growth in population we ought to be planning now to provide not only for the needs of our present population but of our future population.
In the United States they are aware of the situation. Earlier this afternoon some reference was made to the highway program to the south of us. Without going into details with regard to their program, I may say that one thing is clear. They at least look ahead 20 or 30 years and they recognize the increasing need for more and better highways. But what is this government doing?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY

They sit idly by. In conformity with their usual practice when they are confronted with a problem of some considerable magnitude, they avoid dealing with it as long as they possibly can and when finally they are forced into the position of doing something, they come along with legislation which meets only one tiny fraction of the need.
Certainly no one can argue that the trans-Canada highway program brought forward by this government has met any great need in Canada. In so far as it goes, it has assisted the provinces to build highways on the route of the trans-Canada highway. But I think none of us could be overly satisfied with the progress shown thus far. The

government are now proposing to bring forward new legislation which they say will considerably ease the problem. Like other hon. members I am going to say that, in so far as it goes, it is worthy of support. Certainly it is inching a little bit in the direction of the type of policy we need. However, I would be loath to think that the government are advancing this legislation as the answer even this year to the highway needs of Canada.
As far as the present proposals are concerned, I think the payment of 90 per cent of the construction costs of 10 per cent of the trans-Canada highway in any one province is perhaps going to do something to even up the balance or to correct the shortcomings in the original legislation. We hear a great deal about this 50-50 proposition, the federal government putting up 50 per cent of the cost and the provinces 50 per cent. But I think we know that in actual practice it is more like a 60-40 proposition, with the province putting up 60 per cent and the federal government perhaps putting up in the neighbourhood of 40 per cent.
In connection with the purchase of the land necessary for the right of way, we know that a heavy financial burden is thrown on the shoulders of the provinces themselves. The federal government insist-and I think rightly so-on a minimum right of way, but at the same time they refuse to measure up to their responsibilities and pay their share of the cost of this right of way. We know that today, in view of the great number of highway accidents and grade level crossing accidents, it is important that wherever possible we should build overpasses and clover leafs wherever traffic is particularly heavy. But what happens? Under the regulations the federal government is not prepared to participate in meeting the cost of the approaches to those necessary parts of a highway system. The limitation, which I believe is 50 feet on either side of the centre line, certainly makes it impossible for the province to go ahead and put in overpasses in many cases and is certainly inadequate in the case of the clover leafs.
It would seem to me that the government, having failed to pay 50 per cent of the construction costs of the existing trans-Canada highway, is now evening up the score a little bit by providing a little more financial aid to the provinces with respect to this 10 per cent of the highway mileage within the province. But I think the actual increase would amount to somewhere in the neighbourhood of 4 per cent or 5 per cent of the total over-all costs. Hence I think you will agree, Mr. Chairman,
16, 1356	2953
Trans-Canada Highway Act that in this proposed legislation the government is not going overboard in providing greater assistance to the provinces.
In so far as the legislation is concerned, I think we must also realize that the federal government have a financial obligation toward the construction of highways in this country because they are, of course, taking a great deal in the way of revenue out of the sale of automobiles and trucks in Canada. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian Automobile Chamber of Commerce put out a little booklet with which 1 am sure most hon. members are familiar. It is entitled "Facts and Figures of the Automobile Industry".
In this publication they outline quite clearly the tremendous increase in the number of automobiles and trucks in Canada. On page 26 they give statistics with regard to revenues obtained by the government in the form of sales and excise taxes. I note here that for 1954 an amount of some $66 million-that is in round figures-was taken in through the sales tax and close to $72 million through the excise tax, making a total of roughly $138 million during 1954. Since the federal government is obtaining considerable revenues from the motorists in Canada, I think it has a particular responsibility to provide a greater measure of assistance to the provinces in building the roads necessary for these cars to travel on.
As to the extent to which the federal government derives benefit from our automobile industry and our tourist industry, I think some other hon. members this afternoon have pointed out that better highways will bring about greater returns to the federal government. There is no question but that as our population increases we are going to have more and more cars and trucks on our roads. This situation, of course, is going to be reflected in higher receipts by the federal government through the sale of these vehicles. It would therefore seem only proper that the federal government should be prepared to substantially increase its contributions to the provinces for the purpose of building more highways.
What about our tourist industry? Canada's tourist industry is of considerable importance to our economy. There is little doubt that better highways are going to do much to encourage a heavier flow of tourist traffic into this country; and of course the more tourists we get into the country, the more money is going to be spent here and the better off we as Canadians will be.
As far as our own motoring public are concerned, there are many Canadians who would be quite happy to see Canada first
2960	HOUSE OF
Trans-Canada Highway Act if they could get around and see it. But at the present time the situation is that persons going from one part of Canada to the other find that they are obliged to travel on roads which simply do not compare with the highways built by federal money south of the line.
It is apparent that we are missing the boat and are losing a great deal of our own tourist trade. I have reference to Canadians travelling from one part of Canada to another. It seems to me that if we had a greater number of hard-surfaced highways in this country we would increase the number of Canadians who visit other parts of Canada. I think that is something we all desire.
As I suggested earlier, the proposed legislation merely scratches the surface. The problem is immense, and with the growth in population it will become more acute. This trans-Canada highway legislation has failed to do the type of job we think it should have been doing, largely as a result of the fact that too much of the burden was left on the shoulders of provincial governments. I think the Newfoundland member who spoke a moment ago was quite correct when he pointed out that it is unfair to expect provinces with sparse populations to pay one-half the cost. I suggest we are going to have unfairness to many provinces in Canada as long as the federal government is trying to get out from under its responsibility and throw so much of the burden on the shoulders of the provinces.
This afternoon some reference was made by my colleague the hon. member for Assiniboia to United States policy. There will be no need for me to repeat those arguments but I do want to suggest that, taking a leaf from their book, the least we could expect in Canada would be that the federal government would undertake the completion of one highway. I would not be satisfied with that, but it seems to me that in many parts of this country the least we could expect of the government would be the completion of one highway now, on its own initiative and bearing full financial responsibility. I know that in my province there are two main east-west arteries, both of which are exceedingly important. One is the highway which runs from Winnipeg up through Minnedosa, York-ton, Saskatoon, North Battleford, Lloyd-minster and on up to Edmonton. There is a very important east-west artery running through three prairie provinces. Then we have the present route of the trans-Canada, an exceedingly important east-west artery. These two roads certainly ought to be the responsibility of the federal government.
Then there are the north-south roads connecting the United States and Canada.


Certainly the federal government ought to be prepared to take responsibility for building international highways. I suggest that the provinces have all they can handle in providing highways that connect the main cities and towns within a province. Any time a highway becomes primarily an artery between provinces or from one province to the United States, then the federal government ought to be prepared to undertake responsibility for that road.
I suggest that there are two positions which might be taken in this connection. The position taken in former years by the federal government-they relented to a slight degree in the trans-Canada highway legislation- was that the federal government would ignore its responsibilities and persist in an attitude which is 50 years behind the times, that the provinces are responsible for highways. This is an untenable position if there ever was one at the present time. As I suggested before, it might have had some validity back in 1867 or 1890, but it certainly has no validity whatever in 1956.
I suggested the one extreme position would be for the federal government to take no responsibility at all for roads. The other extreme alternative would be for the federal government to step into the picture and do a bang-up job. It seems to me, however, that the least we as members of parliament ought to expect from the government is that they take a middle position and accept responsibility for the main interprovincial highways in Canada, and the international highways. If they do that, then they will leave the provinces free to devote their energies to providing other highways which are long overdue, and to maintaining the highway system which is running far behind present day needs.
This question of highway construction is a problem facing all provinces in Canada. I know that this spring we are having a tremendous amount of trouble in the prairies as the result of a great deal of moisture. This means a great deal of money will have to be spent in maintaining and repairing highways, in some cases rebuilding them. The provincial governments have their hands full in maintaining highways and keeping abreast of local needs without being called upon to meet the heavy financial commitments involved in building a trans-Canada highway.
It seems to me that as an immediate problem we have the proposed legislation and we have the legislation presently on the statute books. I feel that the government, as an illustration of good faith, should be prepared to increase its contribution to at least

75 per cent on the present trans-Canada highway. I believe that is the bare minimum that could possibly be asked of the federal government. This 75 per cent we would ask of the federal government would include all highway costs; the purchase of right of way, the construction of overpasses, clover leafs and the maintenance of the highway in years to come. This is something that could be done immediately.
Then it seems to me that when the present trans-Canada highway is completed there is going to be a need for continued effort on the part of the federal government in co-operation with the provinces. I feel that at this time the government ought to be prepared to announce that on completion of the trans-Canada highway or upon completion of its part by any province, the federal government will be prepared to join with that province in building other main arteries within the province. I believe that would be the bare minimum, and that would only be scratching the surface.
As I suggested, we have a tremendous problem in this country. It seems to me that the government, following the precedent of the United States, ought to take into consideration a complete revision of its attitude toward highway construction. They ought to rid themselves of this archaic idea that because there were no automobiles on the highways in 1867, that lets the federal government out of its responsibility. They ought to be considering a program, as I suggested, based on the assumption by the federal government of the responsibility for building and maintaining the main interprovincial and international highways in Canada.

It is true that great strides have been made in my province on a provincial basis during the past three years, but urgently needed road work is being held up because my province simply does not possess the means to speed up our road building program. We feel that in New Brunswick the trans-Canada highway should consist of two main branches, one running down from Riviere du
Trans-Canada Highway Act Loup in Quebec down through Edmundston, St. Leonard and Fredericton and on through Saint John to St. Stephen; and one coming in from Mont Joli in the province of Quebec on down through the Matapedia valley, through Flatlands, Tide Head, Campbellton, Dalhousie, Jacquet River and on down through Moncton to Amherst.
