The building of that highway, especially in the maritime provinces, has certainly lagged behind the progress made in other parts of Canada. We are placed in an inferior position. We always have to take a back seat. We feel that the federal government should recognize this problem in the maritime provinces for what it is and sit down with the provincial governments and work out a modern, up to date schedule which will take care of the

Trans-Canada Highway Act transportation needs in the maritime provinces for many years to come.
Under the present arrangement it is quite evident for all to see, and it is generally the complaint we meet wherever we go, that no sooner will the trans-Canada highway be built than it will be obsolete, if it is not obsolete before it is completed. All we ask is that more realistic and bold initiative be taken by the federal government to make the trans-Canada highway a realization in fact as well as in discussion which has been going on for so many years.
In closing I wish to say that the people of New Brunswick and the maritime provinces generally feel in regard to the trans-Canada highway and in regard to everything else in the maritime provinces that we are consistently and continually being forced to accept an inferior position. We feel that there has been discrimination against the maritime provinces in connection with the trans-Canada highway. We feel that action should be taken now to make the trans-Canada highway, not only across central Canada but through the maritime provinces-sometimes I wonder if the maritimes are considered to be a part of Canada-a reality.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a few words this afternoon on this resolution because I have always found it hard to understand why Canada does not have a trans-Canada highway, and why Canada did not have such a highway many years ago. For those of us who live on the west coast there seems to be such great value in having a modern highway from coast to coast. By reason of the geography of the country most of our people, when they get into a car to go for a trip, go south to the state of Washington or Oregon or California, and very rarely think of driving east across the mountains. When they want to come east to visit relatives in Ontario, Quebec or the maritimes invariably, for as far back as I can remember, they have driven first to the United States border by the shortest route, driven across the United States and come back into Canada just as far to the east in the United States as possible.
The result, of course, is that all that business is going to the United States, all the contacts are with the towns and various centres of the United States, and they lose the opportunity of getting better acquainted with their fellow Canadians. That has been going on for decades.
Finally in 1949 the dominion government did adopt a policy which was designed to bring about the completion of a modern Trans-Canada highway from coast to coast.


That aroused a good deal of enthusiasm on the west coast. We were all very hopeful that it would result in Canadians of all parts of the country becoming better acquainted, in the building up of national unity, and also in helping our transportation problems. Those provinces, like the maritimes and the western provinces, which are farthest removed from the great centres of Canada have always been bothered by the great costs of transportation, as they are even up to the present time. I could never see why they should not have the benefit of motor transportation on a modern highway. There is no reason why goods should not be carried by trucks right across from one part of Canada to the other, even though it hurts the business of the railways. I think the people who live at the extremities are entitled to that service in just the same way as the people who live in Ontario and Quebec have the great benefits which result from the motor transportation services.
But this plan brought down in 1949 has not worked out as successfully as we all hoped it would. You will remember, Mr. Chairman, that when the agreements were negotiated after this original act had become law, the dominion and each of the provinces that participated agreed that the highway would be constructed by the end of 1956. The minister intimated that when he spoke on Friday last. As recorded on page 2919 of Hansard he said:
The fact remains that they undertook by agreement with us to complete their portion of the highway by the end of the current calendar year.
One would have thought that the provinces would have taken some pains to comply with that agreement, but they have not done so. In the annual report of proceedings under the Trans-Canada Highway Act up to March 31, 1955, which I believe is the latest report available, we find that although the dominion appropriated $150 million for assistance in the construction of this highway in 1949, at the end of March, 1955, the dominion share of the commitments-this was not expenditure but the total expenditure plus commitments-for the highway was only $89,548,291.87. That is not a great deal more than half the original $150 million, and it would be interesting if the parliamentary assistant, when he speaks, would bring that figure up to, say, March 31, 1956.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
I agree that the dominion is not entirely at fault, and I am criticizing the provinces now for the failure to take more energetic steps to complete this highway. Mr. Chairman, I think it is fair to comment that in your own province of Ontario we find the longest gap in the highway. It is true that Ontario has by far the largest mileage of any province. I think it is 1,412 miles, which is over twice that of any other province. Of course Quebec is not included, because Quebec has not become a party under the act. I do not know how long the gap in northern Ontario is now, but the report from which I have been quoting indicates that on March 31, 1955, there was a gap of 162 miles. It does seem to me inexcusable that here in the largest and wealthiest province of Canada there should be the largest gap, where there is apparently no road of any kind.
The parliamentary assistant said a moment ago that the dominion was not at fault. The dominion is very much at fault in this regard, that it is responsible solely for the construction of the trans-Canada highway in our national parks. The same report shows that of the total of 83 miles of this highway which is in national parks, only 47 miles was paved. Just slightly over one-half of the road which is the sole responsibility of the dominion had been paved when there was only another year and nine months before the effectiveness of the act came to an end. It seems to me that the dominion would have been wise to set an example by completing the trans-Canada highway in the national parks rather than by dawdling in just the same way the provinces have been doing.
This whole scheme seems to have been bogged down under a blanket of inertia and indifference. Frankly I cannot understand why that has been the case, but the results indicate that something of that kind has been happening. The resolution indicates that the government proposes to extend the time from the end of 1956 to the end of 1960; to provide an additional $100 million, making the total the dominion government will have spent $250 million rather than $150 million, and finally to give an increased incentive to the provinces by this provision for paying 90 per cent of the cost of the gaps or of the roads of inferior standard up to a total of 10 per cent of the mileage in any particular province.
I doubt if these changes are sufficient to bring about the completion of the highway by
Trans-Canada Highway Act the end of 1960. I hope they will, but I am afraid the dominion is not going far enough, and that more vision is needed primarily on the part of the dominion and perhaps on the part of private members of the house, because the leadership on this question must come from Ottawa.
It seems to me that the dominion's plan is still one of helping the provinces until the road is completed and then dropping out of the picture. In other words, if the dominion's present proposals bring about what it is hoped they will, then at the end of 1960 the dominion government will vanish from the highway picture. The government seems to be accepting no responsibility whatever for essential improvements to the highway as time goes on. A highway today must be of a far better standard than a highway ten years ago, and a highway ten years from now will probably be just that much better and that much more expensive. The parliamentary assistant can correct me if I am wrong, but I believe there is no provision in the legislation for assistance from the dominion in keeping this highway up to modern standards.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
That is just one reason why the provinces are not very keen about the plan, and why the whole plan is breaking down. The dominion should be interested in seeing that this highway is kept up to date. I believe personally that the dominion should also accept some responsibility for costs of maintenance of the highway. I said that during the debate in 1949, and I still believe that would be the proper course to follow.
Then the dominion seems to have no idea whatever of planning any national system of highways. It is only interested in this one trans-Canada highway. Today we hear a great deal about a pipe line across Canada. We are all persuaded that is of great importance to Canada's economy, and we are hoping something is going to be done about it and done quickly. Yet the attitude towards a highway across Canada seems to have absolutely no connection with the attitude toward a pipe line. If the government were as convinced that there should be a trans-Canada highway as it is that there should be a trans-Canada pipe line, then I suggest that the resolution being debated would be a great deal more far-reaching than the one which stands on the order paper at the present time. I do hope that even yet it is not too late for further consideration to be given to the plan which will eventually find its place in the statute books.
The government could well afford to offer a larger contribution to the provinces. Several
2966	HOUSE OF
Trans-Canada Highway Act hon. members who spoke earlier in the debate made that suggestion, and I agree that is one step which would facilitate completion of the highway. The government should also, as I mentioned earlier, make provision for keeping the highway up to date. Once a part has been completed, let the dominion accept some responsibility for seeing that that part will be maintained in the best modern condition.
I think there should also be the inclusion of roads into the north country. The Yukon and the Northwest Territories come under the jurisdiction of the dominion exclusively. They are now in the position that they will be needing roads to connect them with the older part of Canada. Because of the developments taking place in northern Canada, roads into the north are of the utmost importance, and certainly the dominion has a great responsibility with respect to such roads. I suggest that the plans should be extended to cover the key roads which will be serving northern Canada.
There has also been a suggestion that the main roads from the United States border should be in part the responsibility of the dominion. In years gone by that has been the case. I remember the dominion government helping in the thirties with the cost of highways leading from the United States border to national parks in British Columbia and Alberta. I think at that time the dominion paid half the cost of the road from Kingsgate in British Columbia to the boundary of the national park. Some plan of that type should be included under the legislation covering the trans-Canada highway project.
Finally I should like to say a word about the situation in British Columbia itself. We have an available road now and have had for quite a number of years. But, as the minister himself knows, because of the proposal to build a huge dam at Mica creek on the Big Bend a hundred miles or so of the present trans-Canada highway will be flooded, and the province and the dominion are faced with the responsibility of either rebuilding the road or finding another route.
There have been three proposals; one, to rebuild the road around Big Bend; another, to build a road paralleling the route of the Canadian Pacific Railway through Rogers pass and, third, to go down to the south through Kootenay national park, across the Selkirks by means of Jumbo pass and eventually back to Revelstoke again.
The minister seems to 'be taking the attitude that it is not his responsibility to have any part in deciding which of these routes is to be followed. I think he is wrong in that attitude. He should be very much concerned, because there is going to be a great deal of 

money involved. It is going to cost the dominion at least half the amount, perhaps more, and it really is the joint problem and responsibility of the dominion and the province. I hope that before the debate on the resolution is concluded either the minister or his assistant will assure the committee that the dominion is accepting some responsibility for helping to arrive at the best decision as to which of these three routes is to be followed, and that it is not just being left to the province to make that decision. The question is a very difficult one. It is very difficult for the province just as it is for the dominion. The province needs the help and advice of dominion engineers in trying to reach the decision which will be best for all concerned.
I am afraid that the whole trans-Canada highway problem is not being met, largely because of a lack of leadership here in Ottawa, and now that we have a chance to review the whole situation again I hope that much more aggressive steps will be taken than has been the case in the past to bring about the early completion of this project, which I am convinced will mean a great deal to Canadians from coast to coast.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it had not been my intention to take part in this debate. The hon. member for Bow River seemed to think I had made certain interjections. In reality it was one of my more tranquil moments. He suggested that I rise and discuss the route of the trans-Canada highway.
I shall return to the hon. member in a moment. First I want to say that we all want the trans-Canada highway completed as soon as it is financially and physically possible. The only criticism I can see that should be directed at the federal government at this moment would be with respect to their responsibility for construction through the national parks. Admittedly the highway is not completed through the national parks. However, I am quite confident that ere the highway is completed throughout the provinces there will be a highway of first-class proportions through both Yoho national park and Banff national park.
Under the original legislation the federal government responsibility was to provide 50 per cent of the cost of the construction of the trans-Canada highway. So far the provincial governments have not made full use of that financial assistance. At this time the federal government is bringing in a resolution to provide for further assistance in the way of financing, a greater proportion of the cost being accepted by the federal government, namely 90 per cent of 10 per cent of the more costly sections. I see no reason for criticism

directed toward the department with respect to the financing of the highway.
The hon. member for Bow River pointed out that he had been in my riding attending a meeting which, to all intents and purposes, was to discuss a route through East Kootenay and through a portion of West Kootenay to Revelstoke. I am sure the hon. member did not attend any meetings in Edmonton when a decision was being made whether the trans-Canada highway should go through Banff or whether it should go through Yellowhead pass. He probably deemed it advisable at that point to mind his own business. The reason I am not discussing the route at this time is that I am perhaps one of those who would like to mind their own business.
When the agreement was drawn up a route was decided upon. In the report to which the hon. member referred this afternoon, namely "Report of Proceedings under the Trans-Canada Highway Act for the Fiscal Year ended March 31, 1955" there appears an appendix it is appendix B-which sets out the specifications. Apparently the provincial government now is not satisfied with those specifications and is endeavouring to find better bases for highways. I hope they will put them to good use in the sections of the highway that are not yet completed. In appendix A which is headed "Route of the Highway" we find the following:

It goes through the country from Newfoundland to British Columbia, giving the routes that should be followed. For British Columbia we find the following:
From the west boundary of Yoho national park the trans-Canada highway route will follow British Columbia highway No. 1 around the Big Bend of the Columbia river from Golden to Revelstoke. and thence westward through Malakwa, Sicamous balmon Arm and Kamloops following the South Thompson river to Lytton and then the Fraser river canyon and valley route to New Westminster a?d^TVarlcouver- ASain, commencing in the city of Nanaimo on Vancouver island, the route proceeds southward along British Columbia highway No. 1, to reach the city of Victoria, the western terminus of the trans-Canada highway
Then at the end of the appendix there is a further paragraph which reads as follows: In all of the foregoing, where the location of the route is not described in complete detail, the route shall follow the shortest, practical distances successively between the places mentioned. The route may follow the shortest practical diversion around any place mentioned.
I understand that should the provincial governments wish to abandon any of the proposed routes and adopt another route, they should make their wishes known to the
Trans-Canada Highway Act federal authority. It is all very well to say that they need assistance to determine where the route should go, but it is my opinion that the engineering staff of the provincial government department of highways or department of public works, as the case may be, which has the final responsibility for building lateral highways and connecting highways, are in a much better position to determine where the route should go. Once the decision has been made, it is my opinion that when they find some political pressure coming upon them they should not endeavour to throw the blame, if any, on the federal government for one certain area having been overlooked or circumvented. So much for the route.
The hon. member for Bow River has found it necessary to come into the riding of East Kootenay also and to find some defects in the construction of the highway. He had reference to what is known as Kicking Horse bridge No. 1. It appears that test borings were not taken when the bridge was constructed at the confluence of the Kicking Horse river and the Beaver river. While these test borings had not been taken and the bridge showed some defects, it was repaired and the repair which took place on it was work which simply would have been done had the borings been made and had the engineers found the subsurface to be such as it was. The extra cost of the repairs having to be done, or the piling having to be driven after the construction of the bridge, amounted to some $2,000, the over-all reconstruction cost amounting to $54,000.
The hon. gentleman did not go far enough west to go into full detail or he might have found some engineering defects in another part of the highway. The section to which I refer is the part at Park bridge. As we all understand, the engineering and the construction of the highway is the responsibility of the provincial governments, the federal government providing its 50 per cent share. At this particular bridge abutments were placed and certain excavations were continued. Then, of course, there was further construction on that portion of the road leading from the bridge. A landslide took place, and perhaps that could have been avoided if proper engineering data had been available. The over-all cost of making these repairs amounted to $190,000 for removal of the slide and $41,000 for replacement of the abutment to the bridge, a total of $231,000.
I am just mentioning this, and I am not blaming anyone. I can assure the hon. member that if he wants to go from place to place along the highway or look over any construction job, he will find that difficulties arise.

Trans-Canada Highway Act
Certainly very grave difficulties arise when one is constructing a highway through sections of British Columbia where the road runs along the side of a mountain. I do not think anyone should be blamed. I feel it ill behooves the hon. member to bring up this question. He was also concerned because the federal government had not completed its section of the highway through the parks. It just occurred to me that during the period construction has been authorized, the federal government has built a highway from Coleman to Banff for the province of Alberta. This is the eastern slope forest conservation highway, which cost in the neighbourhood of $10 million. The responsibility for this highway really lay with the provincial government, but because of the federal government's desire to help the provinces conserve their forests and their resources, the federal government built this highway. I am sure if there had been any indication that there would be a through connection from Calgary to Vancouver within a year or two, the highway would have been completed. I can assure you also that with the $11 million being spent this year in Banff and Yoho parks, the trans-Canada highway through those parks will be finished long before the provincial sections are completed.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
I have listened with considerable interest, Mr. Chairman, to the list of engineering errors as they were put on the record by the hon. member for Kootenay East. I am sure he must have been in Ottawa a little too long, because in British Columbia we now have a minister of highways who looks over the highways every week end. He has several planes at his disposal. I am sure the hon. member must have obtained his information from some unreliable source, because with one minister flying aeroplanes to look over our highways, I am sure such a grave error could not occur.
However, speaking more seriously-although I do not want to intimate that these plane rides are not a serious matter to the people of British Columbia-I think the manner in which we are asked to deal with this resolution is typical of the progress on the trans-Canada highway. Today is April 16, 1956, yet the latest annual report available on the trans-Canada highway deals with the fiscal year ended March 31, 1955. I am sure that if the minister or his advisors had intended us to have a serious or intelligent discussion of this resolution, the members of the house could have been supplied with more up-to-date information.
I find another thing to criticize in this report. That is, I fail to see amongst the


numerous detailed tables here any information on exactly how many miles of highway are yet to be completed in each of the provinces. I see that table I tells us how much paved mileage each of the provinces had on the designated route at the time of the signing of the agreement. Then I find further tables showing how many miles were paved last year, and also how many miles have been paved since December 10, 1949. However, nowhere do 1 find a table indicating to members how many miles of road each of the provinces has yet to complete, and this was back in March, 1955. I feel that for members to properly assess the situation, since one summer of building has gone by, we ought to have been supplied with this information before we were asked to undertake a discussion of this resolution.
Unlike the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska I feel that coming from British Columbia I cannot plead that our province is such a poor province it can do nothing about building the trans-Canada highway. However, highway building costs in British Columbia are very high. In places they run well over a million dollars a mile. I was therefore rather pleased to read in a newspaper some time ago that the federal government was offering a new formula and, as I understood, were going to assume 90 per cent of the cost of any 10 per cent of the mileage in that province. I believe when the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra spoke he said 10 per cent of the remaining portion of the highway. I do not think he meant to say that, but if I am in error I hope the minister will correct me very shortly. I understand it is 10 per cent of any section of the highway on the designated route within the province, and not 10 per cent of the remaining unbuilt portion of the highway in any given province. The interpretation of this provision makes a great deal of difference in our province. I am willing to give the minister the benefit of the doubt, and assume he is going to ask for authority to pay 90 per cent of the most expensive 10 per cent of the 600 miles we have in this national undertaking.
I feel that the publicity released at the time the change was announced was somewhat misleading. A number of people have asked me if the federal government is going to pay 90 per cent of the cost of the trans-Canada highway. Most of the publicity concentrated on the 90 per cent, but if you read the fine print you found the federal government was making no such offer at all.

Mr. Chairman, before the house rose at six o'clock I was saying, in relation to the ability of the provincial governments to pay their fair share of the cost of the trans-Canada highway, that it was a matter of some concern to the people of British Columbia that their local minister of highways charged to the expense of highways his weekly visit to attend to some parish pump matters in his home riding.
I was saying, too, I regretted that the report of the trans-Canada highway is a year later than was necessary, and that its lateness blocks us from being informed of what has happened on this subject over the past year. I also feel that the report itself could have been more adequate, and that information concerning what remains to be done is missing.
I regretted also that the publicity given the whole matter of the trans-Canada highway project within recent months has led many Canadians to believe that henceforth the federal government will be paying 90 per cent of the cost of the trans-Canada highway, whereas in effect it will be paying only 90 per cent of 10 per cent of the mileage in any one province, and only 50 per cent of the remainder. I made mention of the fact that I came from one of the wealthier provinces of Canada and that we therefore could not plead the poverty which some of the provinces might rightfully be pleading at this time.
I would like now to proceed to point out that despite the fact that we are one of the wealthier parts of Canada, even the Social Credit government in British Columbia is unable to find as much money for highway building as it thought before its election it would be able to find. I am referring to a pamphlet issued May 28, 1952, called the Canadian Social Credjter. This pamphlet was, I think, largely responsible for their winning the election at that time. Under public works it says they will carry out all capital expansion on a-and this is in quotation marks-pay as we go basis. The sentence continues:
. . . priorities being determined by long-range planning and assessment of need.
Underneath that paragraph it says:
Roads should lead to progress-not to bankruptcy.
Even that government has found, after several years in office, that highways are mighty expensive projects these days. They had to invent what they call the toll bridge and road authority. They found they could not allocate enough out of their current
Trans-Canada Highway Act revenues to pay for all the necessary roads and bridges in the province. I therefore imagine they will very much welcome any relief the minister offers to the provincial governments in this resolution.
I feel that it is the responsibility of the federal government to assume a larger share of the cost of this national highway. It is in the national interest to tie this country more closely together from east to west. I would like to say again what I said in this house several years ago. The federal government should assume the responsibility for the building and maintenance of all highways that run east and west from one province into another, and for all highways that run north and south over the international border. I feel that it is in the national interest for it to do so. I do not think there is anything in the British North America Act that would block its efforts to assume complete responsibility for all interprovincial or international roads. If it did so the provincial governments would be enabled to assume the responsibility for all secondary highways, thus relieving the municipal governments of secondary highways and enabling the municipal governments to more ably look after market roads and access highways.
I noticed that the parliamentary assistant to the minister interrupted the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra this afternoon and informed him that the commitments of the federal government no longer are what they were said to be in its annual report. In other words the federal government's commitments amount to $111 million instead of $89 million. That is an increase or growth in one year of federal commitments by the sum of approximately $22 million.
Despite this fact, the minister when talking on his estimates the other day said he had put into his estimates for the year ahead the sum of $20 million, even less than what was added to the commitments of the federal government in the year just past. He also said he would be happy to know that the provincial governments would make him use that full amount. He said he would be very happy to think he might be able to increase it. The fact that his $20 million is less than the $22 million growth in federal commitments last year reveals to us that even with the amendments it is now planning to offer, the federal government is not expecting any miracles or any rapid advance in the development of the trans-Canada highway. If he thought his amendment would have any real effect, I think the minister would have provided for a much larger sum in his estimates this year.

At this time I would like to mention the alternate route of the trans-Canada highway in western Canada. We feel that the trans-Canada highway, when looked at on a map, should have somewhat the shape of the letter "Y" with the ends closed. In other words we feel that in Winnipeg there should be an alternate route. Not only should Vancouver be connected to Winnipeg through the southern portions of Canada where the greatest population is in the four western provinces; we also feel that from Winnipeg there should be a branch of the trans-Canada highway going northwestward through Saskatoon, Edmonton, and the Yellowhead pass and coming down either through the Fraser canyon or Pemberton Meadows, and up around Garibaldi park through North Vancouver and to our major city there. We feel the population out west is so widely scattered that one highway is not sufficient to meet the national needs of that major section of Canada. We also feel that the northern route is badly needed for the development of Canada's northland.
I believe that the federal government would be money ahead in the long run if it assumed at least 50 per cent of the cost of that northern route, because the industrial development of the northern sections of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan would add a tremendous amount of revenue to the income of the federal Minister of Finance. I feel therefore that in its own selfish interests, if not in the national interests, the government should agree that the Minister of Public Works obtain permission to complete a double trans-Canada highway at least as far east as Winnipeg.
Last fall it was my good fortune to be able to attend for a day a course which was put on by the civil defence people in Burnaby. I noticed that one of the major points in the educational endeavours of civil defence organizations in Canada is the evacuation of major Canadian centres of population. I submit it is an absolute waste of money for the Minister of National Health and Welfare to be advocating evacuation through the civil defence branch if at the same time the Minister of Public Works assumes no responsibility as to ways and means-"ways" is a very proper word to use-of evacuating these people. maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we welcome the introduction of this particular resolution dealing with amendments to the Trans-Canada Highway Act. We have listened today to a number of speeches, some of which have been constructive and responsible and other more recent ones which have been destructive and irresponsible.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext: Here we get one more of that kind.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext: What is this coming up?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
If that is so then it fits in with the C.C.F'ers. This afternoon the hon. member for Kootenay East criticized the hon. member for Bow River for referring to some proven facts relative to a certain bridge in the national park in Alberta. He countered with some speculations regarding another construction job on the provincial part of the nighway. The hon. member said that perhaps if the engineers' survey had been carried out as it should this might not have happened.
Then with respect to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, I can only say that I was rather surprised at the sneak attack he launched. The New Westminster 67509-188
Trans-Canada Highway Act paper which I have in my hand refers to a particular meeting at which the minister of highways for British Columbia spoke relative to the unfounded charges which the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has reiterated just now. After stating his position and refuting the charges he said that until someone suggested a quicker method of travel than flying he would continue to fly. He was not challenged at the conclusion of that meeting with even one question. Among those attending that meeting were some of his strongest critics with respect to this particular matter to which reference has been made in this last speech.
So I would suggest, in view of the fact that the British Columbia government is anticipating a $1 billion expenditure for highways in the next ten years, they certainly should be commended rather than criticized in this particular manner. Perhaps I should say, Mr. Chairman, even in politics let us be a little fair and not try to substitute fantasy for facts.
We have been speaking about the importance of highway construction, and it is supposed to be with reference to this one major construction project, the trans-Canada highway. I realize and we all realize the importance of highway construction in this great country of ours. This has been indicated by many of the members who have participated in the debate, but I think there are several reasons why this matter of the trans-Canada highway is of vital importance.
I think it is important so that Canadians may see Canada. I venture the suggestion that a great majority of Canadians travelling from the west to the east or from the east to the west make detours through the United States rather than try to cross Canada on the highway we have at the present time. We may talk as we like about our great nation, and we may try to promote national pride, but certainly we would have to have a great deal of national pride to try to travel over Canadian highways if we were in a hurry to get from one part of the country to the other. So I would say that for Canadians to see Canada, and not for Canadians to see the United States particularly, I helieve the construction and completion of the trans-Canada highway is of vital importance.
I believe also that it is important as far as the tourist traffic is concerned. I understand that in 1954 the value of tourist traffic to Canada was in the neighbourhood of $302 million. I believe that would be substantially increased if we had highways in Canada that the Americans would consider even on a par with those they have south of the border. May I say I have travelled on some

Trans-Canada Highway Act roads south of the border that are not too good, but even at that they are considerably better than our Canadian highways.
Also in connection with the development of our economy, and for purposes of national defence, I believe it is important that this project be brought to completion at the earliest possible moment. There is another reason, I believe, why it should be proceeded with, and not only the one highway but other highway construction projects as well. That is because of the contribution such projects make to optimum employment. We think of all the other trades, we think of all the other industries that provide the essential materials for highway construction, bridge building and so on, and also machinery. I am sure it would mean a great deal as far as the employment picture is concerned.
So I would suggest that these considerations warrant federal participation not only in the trans-Canada highway but in several east-west highways, especially in the west, as well as other arterial highways designed to provide an adequate road system throughout the entire nation. Reference has been made to the Yellowhead route, possibly branching out from Winnipeg or Portage la Prairie, going up through Minnedosa and Saskatoon and through to Edmonton and to the coast by that central route. Certainly I think they have a very fine argument for the construction of that section of a highway system.
I have stated that federal participation certainly is warranted in all these developments. I should like to refer to the submission of the government of the province of British Columbia to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. On page 26 we read:
British Columbia submits that highways which serve to develop the country and thereby add to the gross national product are now matters of national concern and should be financed jointly by the federal and provincial governments; that participation by the federal government should not be confined to the trans-Canada highway but should also be extended to an approved main trunk highway development program in the provinces; that federal participation should be based on a formula which will make allowance for topographical and other conditions which contribute to higher construction and maintenance costs and to a larger road mileage; and that the Trans-Canada Highway Act be amended to provide for a retroactive increase in the federal share of the costs based upon the said cost differential.
I should like to refer as well to the brief presented by the Canadian Automobile Association. I realize the desire to get this resolution passed and I do not want to occupy too much time in this particular debate, but I should like to refer to this brief concerning

Canadian highways presented to Hon. R. H. Winters, Minister of Public Works, by the Canadian Automobile Association. On page 1 in the second paragraph, it states:
The association believes that the federal government is not fulfilling its obligations to the car owners of Canada. The federal government collects through taxation from car owners millions of dollars every year. The return to motorists in roads and improved highways is only a small fraction of the amount collected. The Canadian motorist is awakening to the fact that he is the most heavily taxed individual in Canada. This burden he has long borne without complaining. He is now asking why Canadian highways are so far below present-day needs when taxes are so high.
It also goes on to give a number of precedents, setting forth other fields in which the federal government has made substantial contributions. Then with respect to the tax collected by the federal government we find on page 3:
We would like to mention here that in the first seven months of this year the federal government collected from the automobile industry in sales and excise tax the sum of $116 million, while federal participation in the national highway program is only $15,750,000 for the same period.
This brief goes on to make certain requests of the federal government which I believe are worthy of consideration. On page 7 it states:
The Canadian Automobile Association therefore asks the federal government to;
1.	Assume more responsibility and leadership in developing a highway program.
2.	Instigate an entirely new highway financing policy by: (a) Completing the trans-Canada highway. (b) Contributing 50 per cent to all arterial highways, (c) Assuming one-third the cost of access roads to urban centres.
Respecting my own province, I think it is readily agreed that in British Columbia we have an exceptionally high cost for highway construction. 1 believe it has already been pointed out in the debate that in certain sections of British Columbia the construction of a trans-Canada highway costs approximately $1 million per mile. Certainly that is a tremendous amount, but it just indicates the difficulties they face in the construction of this highway in the province of British Columbia. It is estimated, I believe, that highway construction there costs twice as much as the average cost across Canada, and several times the cost of construction in the prairie provinces.
I should like to refer to the resolution and point out several inadequacies which are obvious. First of all, it refers to the payment of up to 90 per cent of the cost on 10 per cent of the highway. This particular point was referred to by several speakers this afternoon, and I do not think it has been clarified yet by the minister as to what 10 per cent is involved. The point I should like to have

clarified is this. Is the federal government going to choose the 10 per cent upon which it is going to pay 90 per cent, or is the provincial government going to be allowed to make the choice?
I should like to refer to a news article that appeared in the press some time ago, dated November 15, 1955. It contains this brief statement:
But there's a catch. Ottawa will reserve the right to select the 69 miles-
This is in the province of British Columbia, -on which it will boost its share.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext: What paper?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
This is the Province. I do not know whether or not that is right, but I should like the minister to clarify whether it is going to be the federal or the provincial government that will make the choice of the 10 per cent of the mileage with respect to which 90 per cent of the cost will be borne by the federal government. Personally I feel that 10 per cent is not adequate. I believe it should be considerably more than that. In fact I would go along with the suggestion that the federal government should pay at least 90 per cent or even 100 per cent of the cost of the trans-Canada highway.
I believe also that the highway now under construction is not going to be adequate to meet the needs of even the immediate future. It would seem to me quite reasonable to suggest that in certain sections a four-lane highway should be constructed at the present time, and that throughout the entire length provision be made so that in the future two more lanes can be added to make it a four-lane highway right across Canada.
I feel very strongly that the suggestion regarding a trans-Canada highway system should also be given thorough consideration. I am not going to refer to the location of the highways that would make up such a system, but certainly I believe that one highway is not adequate to meet the needs and demands of the Canadian people or the Canadian economy at the present time.
The government has not seen fit to bring in further proposals, and in my opinion those before us at the present time are inadequate. I believe the entire system of financing could be on a better basis, and I certainly urge the government to adopt policies which will enable parliament to use the national credit to provide and finance these services which are so essential to the Canadian people.

That portion of the highway is completed; therefore I have no particular criticism to make. However, I should like to point out one thing. In listening to the discussion of the resolution this afternoon, I was very much interested in what members from various sections of the house had to-offer by way of suggestions to the government on this particular matter. I think all members will appreciate that we have had an across the board assessment of the highway problem of Canada.
The highway problem of Canada is much akin to very many other problems that we who live north of the 49th parallel must face. From time to time many comparisons have been made of the Canadian economy and the economy south of the 49th parallel. Comparisons have been made of the grain marketing problems on one side of the parallel compared with the problems on the other side. I submit that our highway problem has also been compared with that of the nation to the south of us, from the point of view of what it is doing and what we north of the 49th parallel are doing.
I have emphasized before that geographically and climatically we north of the 49th parallel are in a different position from our friends to the south. The same thing is true of highway construction. As I said at the outset, I have no complaint to make. The part of the highway running through my constituency is completed, and I think Saskatchewan leads all of Canada in mileage completed. But that again is because of the geographical conditions and the terrain of Saskatchewan.

As pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's, it is much cheaper to build the highway on the prairies than in certain other parts of this 4,600-mile route, and that must be borne in mind. We are progressing quite well, I believe, and the Minister of Public Works as an engineer recognizes the geographical, climatic and financial difficulties the federal government would face in assuming the full cost of the trans-Canada highway.

The view has been expressed on both sides of the house, and I agree with it wholeheartedly, that the nation as a whole, the taxpayers as a whole, Canada as a whole, should assume the cost of the transcontinental highway. I agree with that statement but I would point out one thing that has not been referred to yet. Any government of Canada, whether it is this government which is in power now or any government of the future, will have to receive a mandate from the taxpayers of Canada before adopting a policy of total assumption by the government of Canada of responsibility for the building of a trans-Canada highway.
I am very happy to hear from all sides of the house that there is general agreement that there should be an assumption on the part of the people of Canada of responsibility for the construction of a highway across Canada. I feel quite sure that when again the people are asked for a mandate as to the policies that are to govern this nation, they will probably be asked whether they are in favour of having the people of Canada, through their government, assume responsibility for a trans-Canada highway; and I shall do whatever I can to see to it that this is one of the things the people are going to decide upon at the next federal election.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a few words in connection with the trans-Canada highway. After listening to the hon. member who spoke last and the sentiments he expressed, I am confident that he probably has the right idea when he suggests that the trans-Canada highway should be in full charge of the federal government. They should have full responsibility for both its construction and upkeep. In that way, and in that way only, can we get the trans-Canada highway through in a decent time. However,
I was shocked today to hear that only 35 per cent of the trans-Canada highway has been built to date. I was really shocked, because I had hoped that at least 75 per cent of it would have been finished to date. We have not had a progress report, so we did not know.
However, I would point out that British Columbia is away ahead of 35 per cent. As the hon. member who spoke last has pointed out, some of our roads were constructed at the cost of $1 million a mile. If that is the case, there is something lacking in the way of idealism in connection with the trans-Canada highway. I blame that on government policy. They have not enthused the various provinces with what is possible with a trans-Canada highway in the way of the great growth of commerce between the various provinces. [DOT]	*


We in British Columbia stand to gain, I admit, if we have one decent road running east and west whereby we could transport our fruit and vegetables without, as at the present time, damaging them more than the cost of the trip from the Okanagan valley, for instance, to the prairies. When we have a decent road I am satisfied that we shall do much better with regard to our prairie market.
As someone suggested this afternoon, I often wondered whether the railway companies are not interested in holding back the trans-Canada highway. I am not going to suggest that that is so. However, another hon. member did so. I remember that, 30 years ago when we wrere trying to get the Hope-Princeton road built from the Okanagan valley to Vancouver, the railway companies were much opposed to it. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company particularly took steps to oppose that particular highway, and it was only after pushing them aside and getting them more or less in agreement that the road was built. However, they offered opposition for a long time. I am afraid there, is something in what the hon. member said this afternoon when he suggested that some influence is at work in preventing construction of the trans-Canada highway.
I would also suggest that in these modern days a two-lane highway is not satisfactory. I think in British Columbia you will find that everywhere possible we shall have a four-lane highway. I would suggest that with the added cost, the federal government should be prepared to increase its offer to the provinces in order to bring the standard highway up to four lanes.
What I particularly want to mention is the fact that we in British Columbia have a slightly different problem, probably, from that in the other provinces. We have east to west roads going through narrow ravines and valleys. In British Columbia we have a situation not paralleled in the rest of the provinces. I refer to the Fraser canyon. We have spent $2 billion a year preparing for the defence of Canada. We have spent it and no one has grumbled. But I often wonder whether we are not foolish in our policy of defence or whether we have grasped the significance of the bottleneck in the Fraser canyon. We have the main trans-Canada C.P.R. line going through there and we have the main trans-Canada Canadian National line going through about a couple of hundred yards away; in places they cross each other. In the same canyon within a few feet of the railway is the trans-Canada highway. One well-placed bomb would destroy the whole

communication system from Vancouver into the interior through the Fraser canyon.
For that reason I am going to suggest to the government that they advance the same assistance to the southern trans-Canada highway as they are advancing to the Fraser canyon highway. I think this southern highway would be cheaper. It would be an alternate route, and at no time would Vancouver or the coast be cut off from the interior. In order to get a trans-Canada highway that is feasible all the year round, under war conditions, peace conditions or any other conditions, I think there must be two highways in our province.
I seriously suggest that the minister consider the southern trans-Canada highway. A great deal of work has already been done. There is perhaps just one small portion as to which we would have to negotiate with our United States friends in order to pass through their territory. In the meantime, lacking this trans-Canada highway, our people are traversing, east and west and north and south, mostly United States roads. That is possibly one of the reasons we are influenced today to such a great extent by United States thought and United States capital. It cannot be helped. We are getting closer and closer to them each day through having to pass through their country, stay in their towns and deal with stores in their towns. Obviously we are getting closer.
On the other hand, if you want to go from British Columbia to visit Regina, Calgary or Edmonton you may possibly go through the dust during the summer time, if you like dust. Otherwise you do not think of driving to those places. I would therefore urge the minister to take steps immediately to give a little bit of leadership with regard to this trans-Canada highway, show a little bit of enthusiasm and give a little bit more money and encouragement to the provinces to carry out the project as quickly as possible, before we find it is too late.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say one brief word on this matter. I have often spoken about what I consider to be the inferiority complex of Canadians. I do not know why it is, but for some reason we do not seem to appreciate our own greatness. When I say "our own greatness" I am not talking about our greatness as personalities; I am talking about the greatness of this vast country and what it may become.
I think this government has always been shortsighted in this matter of highways. I think we have not had enough federal aid to the provinces in the matter of roads. We have heard here today of what the great government to the south of us has done. There is
Trans-Canada Highway Act now no major road in the United States in which the federal government of the United States has not a financial interest. Who can say that this fact has not been for the benefit of that great country?
I should like to say something about a federal system of highways in connection with the matter of the promotion of national unity. I would suggest to you that back in 1867 when the question of building the Canadian Pacific Railway was being mooted, one of the great arguments in favour of that scheme was that it would join together Canadians, of whatever racial origin, from one end of this country to the other. I believe the building of the railroad had a tremendous influence in that direction. I am going to ask you, sir, if in these days the existence of a road across Canada, which would make every part of Canada available to every Canadian, would not be a great thing for the promotion of Canadian unity.
If a man in the province of Quebec, for instance, knew that in two or three days by the use of his automobile he could reach Manitoba or Saskatchewan and meet his fellow Canadians there, would that not be a great thing for the promotion of Canadian unity, which I am sure all of us desire? When I say there might be more travel from the east to the west, I have in mind of course that there would be more travel from the west to the east as well, because we in the west need to understand our eastern friends in Quebec or the maritimes, just as our eastern friends need to understand the people in the west.
There is one thing I should like to mention, and that is that I feel we need not one trans-Canada highway but two, and particularly from Winnipeg west. If you look at the geography of that country you can understand why. I can see why, at the present stage of development, one might argue that one Canadian highway would be sufficient across those rocks from Ottawa to Winnipeg, but when you get to Winnipeg and beyond to those vast agricultural plains the trend is already shown by the railroads. We have Winnipeg which is a sort of bottleneck through which everything must go. Then we have the two great national railway lines, one going across the southern part of the country and one striking northwest and going up to the northern part of the country, and both of them ultimately meeting at Vancouver.
If you look at Trans-Canada Air Lines you find exactly the same situation. You do not find simply a single trans-Canada air line following the main line of the Canadian Pacific, but you find another one following the line of the Canadian National Railways up through

Trans-Canada Highway Act Saskatoon and Edmonton. My belief is that a trans-Canada highway up through Saskatoon, Edmonton and the Yellowhead pass is just as important as a trans-Canada highway in the place where it is now located. I think it is something of a disgrace that this country, which was unified in 1867, has not as yet a road over which a Canadian from eastern Canada can reach the west coast while remaining in his own country.
There is a question also of the tourist trade, which is one of our greatest assets. If one begins to do some research into the tourist trade one finds that there is a considerable imbalance in favour of the United States. We find that Canadians are annually spending more in the United States than United States tourists are spending in our country. I would suggest that one might ponder the reason for that. I may be wrong, but in my opinion the greatest reason is simply that the United States has better roads. We Canadians know that when we cross the border into the United States our difficulties cease so far as automobile travel is concerned. I am convinced that if we had better roads we would be able to eliminate that imbalance and reach a state of equality in attracting tourists. Those of us who live in this country often meet United States tourists, and when we ask them if they are going here or there they say they will not take the risk because they have no confidence in our roads.
For these reasons, then, sir, I would urge upon this government that it take more responsibility in creating throughout this country roads under complete federal jurisdiction, or give assistance to the provinces in completing roads which may be considered as passable.

I did not prepare any notes with which to answer all the criticisms that were made on this resolution because I thought every member in this house would approve of it. As hon. members know, this resolution is only seeking authority to introduce a bill. All kinds of information will be available when the bill is up for second reading.
I want to be very brief, Mr. Chairman, because I think all the criticisms I have heard since this resolution was introduced were mainly directed to the part this government has been playing since the introduction of the trans-Canada highway scheme in 1949. There is one thing that has been said upon which I agree with all hon. members, and this has been said on many occasions when bills were


introduced in this house. It is that the government is heading in the right direction. I agree entirely with that. However, there was one criticism made by some hon. members that I cannot accept. It was stated that the fact that no better progress had been made toward the completion of this highway resulted from the appropriation of too little money in 1949. Well, Mr. Chairman, let us look at the facts, and I suppose the facts speak for themselves.
Hon. members will recall that in 1949 we authorized $150 million. Up to February 25 of this year the total federal commitment amounted to $111 million, which means that out of the $150 million we authorized at that time there is $39 million still in the treasury of which the provinces' can take advantage. I do not think hon. members are fair when they say that if no better progress was made it was due to the fact we did not appropriate enough money.
Another criticism which was made, and which is generally made under similar circumstances, was that we were not doing enough. Well, Mr. Chairman, we of course do appreciate the demands that are made upon provincial treasuries, but we also cannot lose sight of the fact that heavy demands are made upon the federal government for national defence and for social security measures. We frequently hear demands to increase social security measures such as family allowances, old age pensions and the pensions of superannuated civil servants. If we are going to meet all the requests that are made by hon. members of the opposition we certainly will have to find new sources of revenue. We will have to be practical and increase taxes. We must not lose sight of that fact.
I simply cannot understand, Mr. Chairman, how hon. members can get up in this house and repeatedly ask for more money and in the same week accuse us of taxing the people of Canada too heavily. We will probably hear that accusation tomorrow when we resume the debate on the budget. Hon. members opposite will say that the people of Canada are too heavily taxed.

The main point is that to build a trans-Canada highway in this country, indeed to create a national system of highways, would be one of the most productive measures this country could undertake; but because my hon. friends opposite cannot see beyond the ends of their noses-unless it be in connection with the political purposes they are trying to serve, when they are very farsighted indeed-they get up and say that to suggest expenditures for this purpose is irresponsible. The simple answer to that sort of criticism is that it is a proper expenditure for productive purposes which will create employment, which will create industry, which will serve the future of this nation. Such expenditures are always justified provided they are based on sound, efficient and sensible grounds.
My hon. friends opposite boast when it suits their purpose of the tremendous increase in the gross national product, but when we suggest that the increase in the gross national product that would follow from these productive expenditures which we advocate would more than take care of the burden of such expenditures, they forget immediately what the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech. My hon. friend says, "Thank goodness he did not say much." It took him an hour and a half to say what he had to say, and I hate to think how long it would have taken him to say something when it took him that long to say nothing. I know my hon. friends are very good at putting hon. members off the track, but we are not going to be put off the track on this issue. The simple issue is first, whether expenditures by the federal government designed to create one trans-Canada road, which is what we are discussing here, and second, the advocacy of expenditures to create an adequate system of national highways, are irresponsible.
If my hon. friends opposite think that suggestions based upon a realistic appreciation of the future of this country and of what is the responsibility of the government in Ottawa in creating and bringing about conditions under which this country can realize that future; if they think that is irresponsible, then we accept the charge. But by the same token my hon. friends are guilty of the charge of shortsightedness, lack of leadership and lack of imagination. It is those characteristics of theirs which have brought this country to the point where unless we are careful, unless we take certain positive steps, not only are we going to find that our own resources have passed out of our control to the control of people in the United States, but we are going to find that in fact the development of the country as a whole and its future are stultified simply because of lack of leadership and action at this level.
In his reply my hon. friend made some reference to the question of infringement on provincial jurisdiction. That is a real problem, the problem of getting agreement with the provinces for a trans-Canada highway and particularly for the larger project of a national highway system. He talked about infringement on provincial jurisdiction, but in this resolution now before us there is a measure of dictation to the provinces such as I would have thought would make my hon. friend hesitate before advancing that criticism against us.
What has happened under the program as we have had it so far? The provinces have been urged to spend money on the construction of a highway along a certain route, and after they have completed construction to specified standards they are entitled to a 50 per cent contribution. Take any provincial government which is a party to this agreement; take especially any of the provinces 67509-189
Trans-Canada Highway Act which are faced with the construction of difficult sections of the trans-Canada highway; speak to them, and they will tell you they have been hard put to spend anything like their portion of the amount which the federal government is anxious to have them spend. The result is that to which I referred this afternoon.
The province of British Columbia has been most conscientious in its efforts to live up to its obligations, its obligation to its own citizens and its obligation under the over-all agreement, to get on with the trans-Canada highway construction. But that province now finds that it is penalized as a result of the 10 per cent proposal. Take the case of a province which has built a large proportion of its highway through difficult mountainous terrain and has left large sections of easier construction to be done later. To use the term which the parliamentary assistant used, those gaps are partly in the low-cost areas. That province will get only 90 per cent assistance when it completes the gaps, which lie partly in low-cost areas.
Another province may have built only the easy sections, leaving the more difficult sections for the future, but that province will receive 90 per cent assistance applied exclusively to the more difficult areas of their construction. It is certainly a fact that British Columbia has already built some of the most difficult sections of its portion of the trans-Canada highway, leaving some of the stretches of less difficulty for future construction. That forms the gap which is under discussion here. Yet we are told, in the words of the parliamentary assistant, that the 10 per cent applies only to the gaps. That is the 10 per cent to which the federal government will contribute 90 per cent. I refer to his words as reported on page 2522 of Hansard.
Here I may say that some of my colleagues were somewhat critical of my suggestion earlier this afternoon that the resolution, in the terms in which we find it, would penalize those provinces which have been most conscientious in their efforts to build the road. These are the words of the parliamentary assistant which, I say, prove the point I was making:
In no province does the gap or the combined lengths of gaps where there is no highway of any kind exceed 10 per cent of the total mileage in that province.
I would hope not. There is no stretch of British Columbia in which there is no highway of any kind. Then the parliamentary assistant continued.

Trans-Canada Highway Act of the mileage. The federal government contribution for these gaps will be increased from 50 per cent to 90 per cent of the cost of construction.
If those words mean what they say, they mean the provinces will only get a 90 per cent contribution with respect to those portions of the highway not yet completed; but if a province has pressed on, as our own province has, in spite of the tremendous difficulties of construction there, and constructed substantial portions in the mountainous and difficult areas, it means that it cannot get 90 per cent for the portions it has completed-even the most difficult ones- simply because these portions have already been constructed; whereas a province that has left its most difficult portions can get this 90 per cent contribution applied exclusively to those portions. Nothing could be more obvious than that there is inherent, in fact there is actually contained, in this proposal, a proposition which will penalize the provinces which have done most in the past to build this trans-Canada highway. So this proposal requires substantial amendment.
In connection with this matter of the national highways system, upon which my hon. friends opposite cast such scorn, I should like to point out that on January 18, in this session, I introduced a resolution which under the new rules has disappeared from the order paper. I should like now to commend it to the government and to the house for consideration generally as an approach toward solving this question of highway construction in Canada. It reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, (a) the requirements of national defence, as well as the need to serve existing and to promote further development of Canada's territory and resources dictate that there should be more than one east-west trans-Canada highway, as well as several main north-south highways to provide connection with routes in the United States and access to Canada's northland; and (b) the cost of providing such an adequate system of highways built to the standards of modern requirements is beyond the resources of the provinces alone, with the result that Canada is not served by any adequate system of highways or even one adequate trans-Canada highway at the present time;
And therefore the government should take into immediate consideration with the governments of the various provinces the advisability of enlarging the scope of the existing trans-Canada highway agreements so as to develop a system of national highways, both east-west and north-south, financed and maintained jointly by the dominion and the provinces on an acceptable and realistic basis.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the speech we heard from the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Public Works, in which he was invited to reply to the suggestions which were made from this side of the house-and indeed to some of the suggestions made from his own side-that there is an 
increasing measure of responsibility which must be borne by the federal government, simply confirms us in the opinion, which has been growing for some time now, that this government is unable to appreciate its responsibilities, and, even if it were able to appreciate them, is completely incapable of taking any action with respect to them.
As I see it, this resolution in its present form, first, is inadequate to deal with the problem; and second, is going to work a discrimination as between provinces with respect to their existing road construction. Therefore, not because it will make the resolution perfect but simply because I can only move an amendment within the scope of the resolution introduced by the government, I move the following by way of amendment:
That the resolution be amended by adding thereto after the words "not exceeding 10 per centum thereof" the following words:
"the portion of the highway to which such increased payment is to apply to be designated by the province."
This would have the effect that the resolution would read as follows in its introductory portion:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act to provide that the Minister of Finance may pay a higher contribution for a portion of the highway in a province not exceeding 10 per centum thereof, the portion of the highway to which such increased payment is to apply to be designated by the province; . . .
Then the province, if it had completed some of its most expensive portions, could say that it will claim against the federal government 90 per cent of the cost of those portions.

There is one point made by the parliamentary assistant which remains to be dealt with, and I should like enlightenment on it. In the course of his reply he entered the defence that we had no right to be critical of the federal government for having failed to carry forward this trans-Canada highway construction on the ground, if I understood him correctly, that in 1949

I think that was the year he used-parliament had voted, he said, $150 million toward this project and that $150 million had not been spent. My understanding is that that was not a supply vote of this house.
I have checked quickly through the estimates for 1949-and I am speaking subject to correction because I checked quickly-and as far as I can find there was no vote of this house of $150 million. There was, as I understand it, a statutory authority in a bill which was passed in 1948, I think, for expenditures by the federal authority up to $150 million if the provinces were able to get on with their portion of the construction up to that amount.
I therefore do not think it would be accurate or fair to the people generally and to the provinces in particular to suggest that there was appropriated and lying, as it were, available in the federal treasury the sum of $150 million, just waiting for the provinces to spend their portion. The truth of the matter is that the federal taxpayers would still have had to raise their portion up to $150 million at any time the provinces had been able to make or had in fact made that equivalent expenditure.
The point then is this, and this is the nub of the criticism. The provinces now find themselves extended to the limit with respect to their normal road commitments, and they are going to be little if any better able to proceed, whether it be 90 per cent or 100 per cent that the dominion government ties strings to and says must be spent within a certain number of years. They are not going to be much better able to complete this trans-Canada highway, because they have their continuing commitments for developmental roads, secondary roads and the improvement of their road systems generally.
